expertInsight: Application Architect is not an exam you book. You earn it by holding four certifications: Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. Once the fourth one is passed, the credential appears on your profile. If you already hold App Builder and Platform Developer I you are halfway there, and the two architect exams are the harder half. Platform Developer I is also the one exam that counts toward System Architect.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Application Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: There is no Application Architect exam. The credential is granted once you hold Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. The work is in those four exams, and the two architect ones are considerably harder than the first two.
bullets: No separate exam. The credential is awarded when all four component certifications are active.
Four exams to pass. Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect.
Each has its own format and fee. App Builder and Platform Developer I are the cheaper pair, and the two architect exams cost more. Check each exam guide for the current figures.
It pairs with System Architect. Hold both, and you can apply for the Technical Architect (CTA) review board.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Most people take Platform App Builder first, then Platform Developer I, then Data Architect and Sharing and Visibility Architect. Prepare for each exam on its own terms and use that exam's practice questions.

examFormat.heading: Application Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: There is no Application Architect exam to book. Here is how the credential works:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: The two architect exams in this set are scenario-heavy. A typical question describes a business requirement and asks which data model, sharing design or build approach fits best.
bestWayToPass: Start with Platform App Builder: Declarative building, the data model and automation basics. It is the gentlest of the four.
Then Platform Developer I: Apex, SOQL, triggers and testing. It also counts toward System Architect, so it is useful twice.
Then Data Architect: Data modelling, large data volumes, master data management and migration.
Finish with Sharing and Visibility Architect: Org-wide defaults, role hierarchy, sharing rules and external access.

certificationCard.description: Application Architect is earned, not tested. You get it by holding Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. The practice questions here cover the data model and sharing topics those exams focus on.

keyConcepts.h2: Application Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Data Modelling and Large Data Volumes
blocks.body: From the Data Architect exam. Choose relationships for how the data behaves, not for convenience. A **lookup** is a loose link where either record can exist alone. A **master-detail** link makes the child depend on its parent, inherits the parent's sharing, and allows roll-up summary fields, but it also means deleting the parent deletes the children. **External objects** show data that stays in another system. **Big objects** hold very large volumes of historical data that is written and read but rarely updated. For large tables, keep queries **selective** by filtering on indexed fields, watch for **data skew** where one parent owns too many children, and plan archiving before volumes become a problem.

blocks.heading: Choosing Between Configuration and Code
blocks.body: Salesforce expects you to prefer configuration and reach for code only when configuration cannot do the job. **Flow** covers most automation, including record updates, guided screens and scheduled work. Code becomes the right answer when logic is genuinely complex, when very large volumes need batch processing, or when you must do something Flow cannot. The architect's job is to justify the choice: configuration is cheaper to maintain and survives upgrades, while code brings test requirements, deployment overhead and a maintenance burden. Questions that offer a custom-built option alongside a standard feature usually want the standard feature.

blocks.heading: Designing Record Access
blocks.body: From the Sharing and Visibility exam. Access is built in layers and each layer can only open access further, never close it. **Org-wide defaults** set the baseline, so start as private as anyone needs and open up from there. The **role hierarchy** gives managers access to their team's records. **Sharing rules** share by owner or by field value. **Teams** and **manual shares** cover individual records, and **Apex managed sharing** handles rules that configuration cannot express. External users follow their own rules, with **sharing sets** for Experience Cloud customers. Object and field permissions come from profiles and permission sets, and they are checked before sharing ever applies.

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns for Applications
blocks.body: From both architect exams and Platform Developer I. Pick the pattern from the requirement: a synchronous callout when a user is waiting, **Platform Events** or **Change Data Capture** when other systems only need to know something changed, **Bulk API** for large scheduled loads, and **Salesforce Connect** when data should stay in the source system. Keep secrets out of code with **Named Credentials**. Remember the callout limits, 100 per transaction and 120 seconds in total, and move slow work into asynchronous Apex so the user is not kept waiting.

blocks.heading: Build Quality: Testing, Deployment and Governance
blocks.body: Across all four exams, the same expectations recur. Apex needs at least 75% test coverage to reach production, and tests should build their own data and assert real outcomes. Changes move through sandboxes, with source control and the Salesforce CLI or DevOps Center for larger teams. Design for bulk from the start, since code that works on one record and fails on two hundred is the most common defect. Keep an eye on org limits and technical debt, and document the decisions behind the data model and sharing design so the next person can follow them.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Application Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Because this credential is four exams, prepare for each separately. These are the themes that run through all of them.

blocks.heading: Data Modelling Choices
blocks.body: Master-detail for dependent children, roll-ups and inherited sharing. Lookup when records stand alone. External objects when the data should not be copied.

blocks.heading: Record Access Design
blocks.body: Start with the most private org-wide default anyone needs, then open access with the role hierarchy and sharing rules. Only use Apex sharing when configuration cannot express the rule.

blocks.heading: Configuration Before Code
blocks.body: Flow first. Code when logic is complex, volumes are large, or Flow genuinely cannot do it, and be ready to justify the choice.

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns
blocks.body: User waiting means synchronous. Others just need to know means events. Large and scheduled means Bulk API. Should not be copied means Salesforce Connect.

blocks.heading: Large Data Volumes
blocks.body: Keep queries selective, avoid ownership and account data skew, and plan archiving before the table gets big.

nextCertsAfter.heading: What to Do After Application Architect
nextCertsAfter.intro: Application Architect and System Architect together are the prerequisites for CTA:

sampleQuestions.question: What is the focus of an Application Architect?
options: Deep understanding of native Salesforce features and modeling role hierarchy, data, and sharing
sampleQuestions.explanation: Application Architects have deep understanding of native Salesforce features and model role hierarchy, data, and sharing.
whyWrong: 'Only Apex' narrows the focus incorrectly to a single language, when the role is about broader native-feature architecture.
Email is unrelated to the Application Architect's data modeling and sharing focus.
Slack is unrelated to the Application Architect's data modeling and sharing focus.

sampleQuestions.question: Which sharing mechanism is used to open access based on record ownership?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Sharing rules extend access based on ownership or criteria.
whyWrong: 'Only permission sets' misattributes ownership-based sharing to a different access-control feature.
'Only OWD' misattributes ownership-based access to the baseline setting, not the sharing mechanism itself.
'Only profiles' misattributes ownership-based sharing to a different access-control feature.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the role hierarchy used for?
options: Inheriting record access and roll-up for forecasts and reports
sampleQuestions.explanation: Role hierarchy controls record access inheritance and roll-up for reporting and forecasts.
whyWrong: CPQ is unrelated to role hierarchy's access-inheritance purpose.
Email is unrelated to role hierarchy's access-inheritance purpose.
'Only reporting' undersells role hierarchy, which also inherits record access, not just reporting roll-up.

sampleQuestions.question: Which certification is typically a prerequisite for Application Architect?
options: Platform Developer I and Sharing and Visibility Architect (or equivalent knowledge)
sampleQuestions.explanation: Application Architect builds on platform and sharing/visibility knowledge.
whyWrong: Marketing Cloud alone is unrelated to the architect-track prerequisite knowledge needed.
Email Specialist is unrelated to the architect-track prerequisite knowledge needed.
Slack alone is unrelated to the architect-track prerequisite knowledge needed.

sampleQuestions.question: What does 'modeling data' mean for an Application Architect?
options: Designing object model, relationships, and data volume strategy
sampleQuestions.explanation: Modeling data includes object design, relationships, and data volume strategy.
whyWrong: 'Only backups' undersells data modeling, which includes object design and volume strategy, not just backups.
'Only reports' undersells data modeling, which is about underlying structure, not display.
'Only dashboards' undersells data modeling, which is about underlying structure, not display.

sampleQuestions.question: What does Organization-Wide Defaults (OWD) control?
options: The baseline record access for each object (Private, Public Read Only, etc.)
sampleQuestions.explanation: OWD defines the default sharing model for each object.
whyWrong: 'Only permission sets' misattributes OWD to a different access-control concept.
'Only roles' misattributes OWD to a different access-control concept — OWD is the baseline setting, not role-based.
'Only profiles' misattributes OWD to a different access-control concept.

sampleQuestions.question: Which mechanism extends access when OWD is Private?
options: Sharing rules, role hierarchy, and manual sharing
sampleQuestions.explanation: Sharing rules, role hierarchy, and manual sharing extend access beyond OWD.
whyWrong: 'Permission sets only' undersells the broader set of mechanisms (sharing rules, hierarchy, manual) that extend access.
'Profiles only' undersells the broader set of mechanisms that extend access when OWD is Private.
'OWD only' contradicts the question, which asks what extends access beyond a Private OWD baseline.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a criteria-based sharing rule?
options: To grant access to records that match specified criteria
sampleQuestions.explanation: Criteria-based sharing rules grant access based on field values.
whyWrong: Criteria-based sharing rules don't create reports — that's an unrelated function.
'To restrict access' is the opposite of what a criteria-based sharing rule does — it extends access.
Criteria-based sharing rules don't assign users — that's a separate administrative task.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Salesforce feature supports multi-tenant data isolation?
options: Sharing model, org ID, and platform architecture
sampleQuestions.explanation: Sharing model and org-level isolation provide multi-tenant security.
whyWrong: 'Permission sets only' undersells multi-tenant isolation, which is a broader platform architecture concept.
'Roles only' undersells multi-tenant isolation, which is a broader platform architecture concept.
'Only profiles' undersells multi-tenant isolation, which is a broader platform architecture concept.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the development lifecycle for an Application Architect include?
options: Design, development, testing, deployment, and governance
sampleQuestions.explanation: Lifecycle spans design through deployment with governance.
whyWrong: 'Only coding' undersells the development lifecycle, which spans design through governance, not just code.
'Only documentation' undersells the development lifecycle, which spans the full process, not just documentation.
'Only deployment' undersells the development lifecycle, which spans the full process, not just deployment.

sampleQuestions.question: Which relationship affects record-level security and roll-up?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Master-Detail affects sharing; child inherits parent's access.
whyWrong: A Junction object uses master-detail relationships, but the underlying mechanism being asked about is Master-Detail itself.
Lookup relationships don't inherit sharing from the parent — that's specifically a Master-Detail behavior.
External lookup connects to external data — it doesn't provide the internal sharing/roll-up inheritance being described.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a delegated admin group?
options: To grant limited admin capabilities to specific users
sampleQuestions.explanation: Delegated admin groups provide scoped admin access.
whyWrong: 'To create profiles' misattributes delegated admin's purpose to a different administrative task.
'To assign permission sets only' undersells delegated admin, which can include broader limited admin capabilities.
Delegated admin groups don't replace the system admin — they extend limited admin capability to specific users.

sampleQuestions.question: Which integration consideration applies to Application Architects?
options: Authentication, data ownership, and sharing for integrated data
sampleQuestions.explanation: Integration must consider auth, ownership, and sharing.
whyWrong: Ignoring security contradicts the core consideration architects must address for integrated data.
'Only REST' undersells the broader integration considerations beyond a single protocol.
'Only batch' undersells the broader integration considerations beyond a single pattern.

sampleQuestions.question: What does visibility mean in the sharing context?
options: Which records a user can see based on sharing rules and permissions
sampleQuestions.explanation: Visibility determines which records are visible to users.
whyWrong: 'Only UI' misrepresents visibility, which is about data access via sharing/permissions, not interface design.
'Only reports' undersells visibility, which is a broader data-access concept beyond just reports.
'Only dashboards' undersells visibility, which is a broader data-access concept beyond just dashboards.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best practice supports scalable role hierarchy design?
options: Keep hierarchy flat where possible; avoid deep nesting
sampleQuestions.explanation: Flatter hierarchies simplify sharing and maintenance.
whyWrong: 'Unlimited depth' is the opposite of the flat-hierarchy best practice for scalability.
'One role only' is impractical and doesn't reflect real organizational structures needing role hierarchy at all.
'No hierarchy' contradicts the fact that role hierarchy is a real, necessary structure for most orgs.
